title: Acquisition of Control - Canadian SR&ED Tax Credit Glossary
description: Learn how an Acquisition of Control affects corporate tax year-ends, expenditure pools, and ITC carryforwards in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: Acquisition of control is a key consideration in Canada's federal SR&ED tax incentive program, because who controls a corporation determines its credit rate under the Income Tax Act. Canadian-controlled private corporations and eligible Canadian public corporations not controlled by non-residents earn the 35% enhanced investment tax credit on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures; foreign-controlled subsidiaries earn only 15%.

body.text: Acquisition of control is a key consideration in Canada's federal SR&ED tax incentive program, because who controls a corporation determines its credit rate under the Income Tax Act. Canadian-controlled private corporations and eligible Canadian public corporations not controlled by non-residents earn the 35% enhanced investment tax credit on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures; foreign-controlled subsidiaries earn only 15%.

Canada operates one of the most comprehensive research and development tax incentive frameworks in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program under Sections 37, 127, and 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (ITA). Between December 2024 and November 2026, this statutory regime underwent its most substantial legislative expansion in more than a decade. Under Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, Parliament doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, increasing the maximum annual refundable federal credit to $2,100,000. Simultaneously, Bill C-15 widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended access to the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue formula, granted Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) an option to elect into that revenue-based phase-out structure, and restored SR&ED eligibility for capital expenditures and shared-use equipment acquired after December 15, 2024. Building on those enacted reforms, Federal Budget 2026 (Masters of our Destiny, tabled November 5, 2026) proposed an additional $930 million five-year expansion ($235 million ongoing annually) for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026, bringing downstream initial regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs into the SR&ED expenditure pool for the first time, subject to legislative enactment.

Sub-national governments concurrently redesigned their provincial R&D tax incentives. Québec eliminated eight legacy R&D tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing them with the fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) at 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding an exclusion threshold and 20% thereafter, while extending eligibility to pre-commercialization product design and regulatory validation. British Columbia enacted Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), making its 10% SR&ED credit permanent, harmonizing with the federal $6,000,000 refundable limit and capital expenditure restoration, and extending refundability to ECPCs. Saskatchewan doubled its 10% CCPC refundable expenditure limit to $2,000,000 and restored capital expenditure eligibility in its March 18, 2026 budget alongside its 6% provincial Patent Box (the Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive), whereas Ontario mirrored the post-December 15, 2024 restoration of capital equipment while retaining its standalone $3,000,000 annual expenditure limit on the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC).
1. Executive Synthesis of Federal Program Evolution (2024–2026)

Canada's federal SR&ED program operates as a dual-pillar tax incentive that industry estimates value at over $4.5 billion in annual support for businesses conducting scientific research or experimental development in Canada. The first pillar allows taxpayers carrying on a business in Canada to pool allowable domestic current and post-December 15, 2024 capital SR&ED expenditures under Section 37 of the ITA, deducting them in full in the taxation year incurred or carrying them forward indefinitely against future business income. The second pillar provides a volume-based Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under Section 127 of the ITA, computed either at the 35% enhanced rate (up to the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit for CCPCs and ECPCs) or at the 15% basic rate (for foreign-controlled subsidiaries, non-eligible public corporations, individuals, trusts, partnership allocations, and CCPC or ECPC expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit). Unused non-refundable federal ITCs carry back 3 taxation years and forward 20 taxation years.

Program administration also shifted substantially in 2026. On April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process through My Business Account, allowing eligible businesses to secure upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks prior to starting R&D work or incurring project costs, while accelerating post-filing review service standards for refundable claims from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days where every claimed project holds pre-claim approval. At the judicial level, despite the CRA's August 2021 shift toward simplified administrative eligibility framing ("Why" and "How" requirements), the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72) that the five-question common-law test established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (1998) remains the binding legal standard across Canada, with National R&D adding that CRA administrative guidelines are not binding on the courts.

body.text: 2. Federal Statutory and Legislative Architecture
2.1 Core Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations Provisions

Canada's federal R&D tax framework is codified in the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945, with legislative policy formulated by the Department of Finance Canada and operational compliance administered by the Canada Revenue Agency. Because SR&ED operates as a statutory entitlement within the self-assessment income tax system rather than a discretionary grant competition, any resident taxpayer—or non-resident carrying on business through a Canadian branch—that incurs qualifying domestic R&D expenditures and satisfies mandatory filing rules is legally entitled to claim the applicable deductions and tax credits.

headers: Governing Legal Subject Matter and Operational Function

Governs the Investment Tax Credit (ITC) regime, including statutory definitions of "qualified expenditure," "government assistance," "non-government assistance," and "shared-use-equipment" (s. 127(9)), annual expenditure limits and associated-corporation rules (ss. 127(10.2), 127(10.6)), and non-arm's length cost adjustments ("adjusted selling cost" and "adjusted service cost" in ss. 127(11.6)–(11.7)).

Sets out the exhaustive statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development," specifying eligible basic research, applied research, experimental development, eight disciplines of direct support work, and seven excluded commercial or routine activities.
Defines arm's length and non-arm's length relationships governing related-party subcontracts, goods and services purchases, and assistance allocations.
Imposes a $1,000 statutory penalty for non-compliance with mandatory SR&ED claim preparer disclosure requirements on Form T661.

Governs prescribed expenditures (s. 2901), disallowed prescribed expenditures for ITC calculation including general administration, legal/accounting fees, interest, society dues, used equipment, acquisition of rights, and donations (paras. 2902(a)–(d)), and special-purpose buildings (s. 2903).

Defines Prescribed Venture Capital Corporations (s. 6700), Prescribed Federal Crown Corporations (s. 7100, distinguishing tax-exempt Crown corporations barred from earning ITCs), and "permanent establishment" (s. 8201, governing taxable supplier status and provincial allocation).

body.text: 2.2 Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Frascati Manual Alignment (Subsection 248(1))

Subsection 248(1) of the ITA defines "scientific research and experimental development" in close conformity with the OECD Frascati Manual as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". Within that overarching requirement, eligible work is divided into three primary research categories and one strictly bounded category of direct support work. Basic research (paragraph 248(1)(a)) comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, whereas applied research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Experimental development (paragraph 248(1)(c))—which represents the predominant basis for private-sector claims in Canada—comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, explicitly including incremental improvements thereto. Crucially, in a commercial business setting, creating a commercially novel product does not automatically qualify; the work must seek to advance the taxpayer's underlying technology base or engineering knowledge beyond standard practice at the outset of the project.

Alongside those three core pillars, subsection 248(1) admits direct support work strictly limited to eight enumerated disciplines: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, and only to the extent that the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development carried out in Canada. Other corporate innovation activities or administrative functions outside those eight disciplines do not qualify. Conversely, subsection 248(1) expressly excludes seven statutory categories of commercial, non-scientific, or routine work: (1) market research or sales promotion; (2) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (3) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (4) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (5) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (6) style changes (cosmetic or aesthetic modifications lacking technological advancement); and (7) routine data collection.
2.3 Chronology of Recent Legislative Reforms (2024 FES, Bill C-15, and Budget 2026)

Tax auditors reviewing corporate filings across the 2024–2027 transition window must carefully distinguish among sequential federal policy announcements, particularly because secondary literature published in late 2024 or early 2025 frequently cites an unlegislated interim $4.5 million threshold. In December 2024, the federal government tabled the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), proposing for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 to raise the enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from $3.0 million to $4.5 million, widen the CCPC taxable capital phase-out thresholds to $15 million–$75 million, extend the 35% enhanced ITC to ECPCs, permit CCPCs to elect into a revenue-based phase-out structure, and restore SR&ED eligibility for capital property acquired (and lease costs first becoming payable) after December 15, 2024. However, parliamentary prorogation and the ensuing federal election intervened before the $4.5 million proposal was enacted.

On November 4, 2025, Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne presented Budget 2025, which retained the December 16, 2024 effective transition dates (taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 and depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024) as well as ECPC access, the $15 million–$75 million phase-out range, the CCPC revenue election, and capital expenditure restoration, while superseding the $4.5 million proposal by increasing the annual enhanced expenditure limit directly from $3.0 million to $6.0 million. Parliament enacted this package through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Between May 15 and June 29, 2026, the CRA released updated prescribed forms (Form T661 (26), T2 Schedule 31, T2 Schedule 49, Form T1145, and Form T1146) and revised policies governing capital expenditures, shared-use equipment, and total qualified SR&ED expenditures.

In autumn 2026, two further federal tax policy developments reshaped R&D capital and commercialization planning. First, on September 15, 2026, the federal government announced the Productivity Mega Deduction (released as draft legislation on October 1, 2026 and confirmed in Budget 2026), proposing permanent immediate 100% expensing for a broad range of eligible capital assets acquired on or after September 15, 2026 (excluding Class 1 buildings, although qualifying manufacturing and processing buildings retain a separate temporary immediate-expensing measure from Budget 2025); Department of Finance estimates indicate the measure covers over 65% of business investment and reduces Canada's marginal effective tax rate on new investment from 13% to 6.4% once enacted. Second, on November 5, 2026, the government tabled Budget 2026 (Masters of our Destiny), proposing a $930 million five-year SR&ED expansion ($235 million ongoing annually) to include initial regulatory certification testing and IP protection costs for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026—meaning calendar-year corporations will first access these commercialization rules in their 2027 taxation year, subject to legislative enactment. Budget 2026 also launched consultations (open until January 8, 2027) on permitting corporate loss transfers of current-year non-capital losses within wholly owned corporate groups, alongside proposing the Canada Growth Incentive (an exemption on up to $15 million of capital gains on eligible Canadian corporate shares) and extending the Clean Technology (30%) and Clean Electricity ITCs to property available for use before 2041.
2.4 Status of Federal Patent Box Proposals vs. Provincial IP Regimes

A critical verification point for cross-border R&D structuring is the absence of a federal Canadian "Patent Box". Although the December 2024 Fall Economic Statement promised details on a federal Patent Box regime and the governing party reiterated that pledge in April 2025, neither Budget 2025 nor Budget 2026 included a federal Patent Box regime or any Notice of Ways and Means Motion to create one, nor was any draft IP income-tax legislation published in the Canada Gazette through November 2026. Instead of enacting a back-end preferential federal tax rate on IP royalty or embedded patent income, Ottawa opted to subsidize commercialization and IP retention through front-end SR&ED credits for IP registration and maintenance costs in Budget 2026, direct funding renewals—including $84.4 million over four years (starting 2026–27) for Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's (ISED) ElevateIP program, $75 million over three years (starting 2026–27) for the National Research Council's IP Assist program, and $22.5 million over three years (starting 2026–27) for the Innovation Asset Collective's Patent Collective—and proposed Patent Act regulations requiring patent ownership changes to be registered with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO) and setting minimum requirements for written patent infringement demand letters. Preferential corporate income tax rates on commercialized IP income exist in Canada exclusively at the provincial level, specifically in Québec under the Déduction incitative pour la commercialisation des innovations (DICI, lowering the provincial rate on eligible IP income from 11.5% to 2%) and in Saskatchewan under the Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (SCII, lowering the provincial corporate rate from 12% to 6% for 10 to 15 years).
3. Federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Rates, Thresholds, and Refundability Mechanics
3.1 Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures and Taxability of Credits

Under Section 37 of the ITA, resident taxpayers (and domestic branches of non-resident corporations) aggregate their allowable domestic current and post-December 15, 2024 capital SR&ED expenditures into the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures. Unlike regular capital assets depreciated gradually via Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) on Schedule 8, the positive balance of the Section 37 pool may be deducted up to 100% against business income in the current taxation year, or any unclaimed portion may be carried forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. Where a claimant elects the Proxy Method for overhead, the notional 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is excluded from the Section 37 deductible pool, although actual underlying business overheads remain deductible as ordinary operating expenses.

Crucially, federal SR&ED tax relief is itself taxable in the subsequent year: used and refunded federal SR&ED ITCs are included in taxable income in the following taxation year (operating first by reducing the Section 37 deductible SR&ED pool in the subsequent year and bringing any excess into income). By contrast, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute current-year government assistance under subsection 127(9) and therefore reduce both the federal Section 37 pool and federal Section 127 qualified expenditures immediately in the claim year unless validly waived or renounced.
3.2 Section 127 Investment Tax Credit Rates and Expenditure Limit Phase-Outs

Federal SR&ED ITCs under Section 127 operate on a pure volume basis across two statutory tiers. The enhanced 35% ITC rate applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the taxpayer's annual expenditure limit—set at $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 ($3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024)—and is restricted to Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) and, post-December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs). An ECPC is defined as a public corporation resident in Canada, listed on a designated stock exchange, and not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons (determined as though all shares owned by non-residents were held by a single person). The basic 15% ITC rate applies with no upper expenditure ceiling to all qualified SR&ED expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs exceeding their annual expenditure limit, as well as to all qualified expenditures of foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries, non-ECPC public corporations, individuals, trusts, and partnerships.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 baseline expenditure limit must be shared across associated CCPCs (allocated on T2 Schedule 49) or across ECPC corporate group members included in consolidated financial statements, and is further reduced for short taxation years or multiple taxation years ending within the same calendar year. Above SME scale thresholds, the $6,000,000 limit phases out linearly to zero across a $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 range ($60,000,000 span) under two statutory mechanisms:

items: Taxable Capital Phase-Out (Default for CCPCs): A CCPC's (and associated group's) $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease once combined taxable capital employed in Canada in the immediately preceding taxation year reaches $15,000,000, declining by $1 of expenditure limit for every $10 of excess taxable capital until becoming nil at $75,000,000 (up from the pre-December 16, 2024 phase-out range of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000).

Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out (Mandatory for ECPCs; Elective for CCPCs): An ECPC's (and consolidated group's) $6,000,000 expenditure limit phases out linearly when average gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years exceeds $15,000,000, reaching nil at $75,000,000. Under Bill C-15, a CCPC (or group of associated CCPCs) may elect to compute its expenditure limit using this identical three-year average gross revenue structure instead of taxable capital, enabling heavily capitalized, pre-revenue or early-revenue CCPC innovators (such as biotechnology or clean-hardware firms whose paid-up capital exceeds $15,000,000) to preserve the full $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit.

body.text: 3.3 Refundability Matrix, Qualifying Income Limit, and Entity-Specific Rules

Under post-Bill C-15 rules, refundability depends simultaneously on the claimant's legal entity classification, whether expenditures fall within or above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, and whether the underlying outlay is a current expenditure or a capital expenditure. Specifically, even at the 35% enhanced rate, capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024 are 40% refundable, whereas current expenditures are generally 100% refundable. Furthermore, whether a CCPC earns a 40% partial refund on excess spending above its expenditure limit (at the 15% basic rate) turns on whether it qualifies as a "Qualifying Corporation"—defined as a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income (combined with associated corporations) did not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit. That Qualifying Income Limit starts at $500,000 when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is below $15,000,000 and phases out proportionally across the $60,000,000 taxable-capital span above $15,000,000, reaching nil at $75,000,000.

body.text: Two structural exclusions frequently arise in corporate audits. First, because a partnership is not itself a taxpayer under the ITA, it cannot claim an SR&ED ITC directly and never earns the 35% enhanced rate; instead, the 15% ITC is computed at the partnership level and allocated to eligible partners, with only partners that are Qualifying Corporations, individuals, or certain trusts eligible for a 40% cash refund on their allocated share. Second, as clarified in CRA's May 22, 2026 Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, SR&ED expenditures incurred by a Crown-owned corporation (other than Prescribed Federal Crown Corporations under ITR Section 7100) are excluded from earning ITCs because the corporation's income is exempt from Part I tax.
3.4 Carryback, Carryforward, and ITC Recapture Provisions

Unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs (beyond amounts applied to reduce current-year federal Part I tax payable to zero) may be carried back up to 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years. Conversely, to ensure tax incentives subsidize only net R&D costs, ITC Recapture Rules apply whenever a taxpayer sells or converts to commercial use: (1) materials whose cost was previously claimed as a qualified SR&ED expenditure; (2) depreciable SR&ED capital property acquired before 2014 or after December 15, 2024; or (3) Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) where SR&ED usage becomes merely incidental and all or substantially all of the asset is converted to commercial use. Recapture adds all or a portion of the previously earned SR&ED ITC directly back to income tax payable in the year of sale or commercial conversion, reported on T2 Schedule 31 (corporations) or Form T2038-IND (individuals). Under Budget 2026 proposals, parallel recapture rules will apply to both the SR&ED deduction and ITC if a taxpayer subsequently disposes of intellectual property for which IP protection costs received SR&ED support.
4. Qualifying Research Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
4.1 Overhead Election: Proxy Method (55% PPA) vs. Traditional Method

Every claimant must elect either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method on Form T661 for each taxation year claimed. Once an SR&ED claim is filed for a taxation year, the chosen method cannot be changed for that year; if a claimant fails to select a method on Form T661, the CRA processes the claim using the Traditional Method.

body.text: 4.2 Salaries, Wages, Specified Employee Caps, and Foreign Labour Rules

Claimable SR&ED labour is strictly restricted to salaries and wages (Canada provides no standalone R&D payroll-tax or social-security contribution exemption) paid to employees directly engaged in hands-on SR&ED. Whether an employee is directly engaged is determined strictly by the tasks performed and actual time spent rather than job title. Qualifying directly engaged tasks encompass hands-on experimentation and analysis; support work within the eight statutory disciplines; non-specialized tasks (such as operating machinery or feeding raw materials during an experimental run) supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications; direct technical supervision of employees performing SR&ED; technical input into SR&ED contract coordination; technological planning and technological feasibility studies for ongoing claimed SR&ED projects; and internal technical documentation.

Strict statutory exclusions govern shareholder-founders, unpaid remuneration, and work performed outside Canada. Dividends paid to owner-managers are not salary or wages and are completely ineligible for SR&ED, and the CRA closely audits above-market founder salaries. For specified employees (governed in detail by CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy and SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy), total claimable SR&ED salary is subject to a 5 × Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) cap, while inclusion in the Proxy Method salary base is subject to a 2.5 × YMPE cap allocated across related entities and partnerships. Furthermore, an asymmetric 180-day unpaid amounts rule applies at year-end: salaries or wages incurred in a taxation year must be paid within 180 days of the end of that taxation year to be allowable SR&ED expenditures (unpaid wages cannot be added back as prior years' unpaid amounts when paid later), whereas non-salary current expenditures (such as contractor invoices or materials) unpaid within 180 days of year-end are deducted from current-year qualified expenditures and added back to qualified expenditures in the subsequent year when paid. Finally, permissible salary or wages for SR&ED physically performed outside Canada may be claimed only where five conditions are met: (1) the work was performed directly by an employee (never a contractor); (2) the employee was a resident of Canada when the expense was incurred; (3) the work related to the claimant's business; (4) the work was an integral part and solely in support of the SR&ED project carried out in Canada; and (5) the amount claimed does not exceed 10% of the claimant's salary or wages for SR&ED directly undertaken by it in Canada (ITA subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)).
4.3 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Transfers, and Third-Party Payments

Canadian tax law enforces distinct rules across arm's length SR&ED contracts, non-arm's length (NAL) arrangements, and third-party research payments. Under an arm's length SR&ED contract, a contractor performs basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible direct support work on behalf of the claimant; the claimant controls the work, retains exclusive rights to the results, and claims costs on an accrual basis. When computing Section 127 qualified expenditures for ITC purposes, 20% of arm's length contract expenditures must be deducted—meaning only 80% qualifies for the SR&ED ITC. Even more importantly, the contractor must be a "taxable supplier" (a Canadian resident, or a non-resident operating through a Canadian permanent establishment under ITR Section 8201); payments to a non-taxable supplier are 100% excluded from qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. As illustrated in Example 9.5.3 of CRA's May 22, 2026 Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, if a Canadian company pays $45,000 ($40,000 fee plus $5,000 reimbursed travel) to an arm's length non-resident individual who has no Canadian permanent establishment—even if the individual performs the R&D physically inside the claimant's Canadian premises—none of the $45,000 earns an ITC, although it remains an allowable Section 37 deductible expenditure. Subcontracted R&D performed outside Canada is wholly ineligible.

By contrast, expenditures under non-arm's length (NAL) SR&ED contracts never directly earn an ITC in the payer's hands. Instead, the NAL performer must file its own Form T661 by its income tax due date and may transfer all or part of its qualified SR&ED expenditures (including its PPA, per Appendix A.2 of CRA's May 2026 policy) to the claimant by jointly executing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length). Where a claimant purchases non-SR&ED goods or services from a NAL supplier, ITA subsections 127(11.6) and 127(11.7) cap the claimant's qualified expenditure at the supplier's actual "adjusted selling cost" or "adjusted service cost". Separate from contracts, third-party payments—made on a cash basis to CRA-approved associations, universities, colleges, research institutes, granting councils, or eligible Canadian-resident/tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations where the performer controls the research, results are non-exclusive (generally published), and the claimant receives a preferential right or entitlement to exploit results related to its business—require filing Form T1263 for each payment and are likewise subject to the 80% inclusion rule (20% reduction) for ITC purposes.
4.4 Materials, Cloud Computing, and Prescribed Disallowed Expenditures

Allowable SR&ED materials comprise physical items consumed (rendered virtually valueless) or transformed (incorporated into prototypes or experimental outputs, subject to ITC recapture upon sale or commercial conversion) in performing SR&ED in Canada. Living things themselves cannot be claimed as materials (though inputs such as animal feed or fertilizers may qualify), while general utilities such as electricity, water, and fuel constitute overhead rather than materials. For software and AI startups, practitioners note that cloud computing expenses (such as AWS, Google Cloud Platform, or Azure environments) dedicated strictly to R&D experimentation, staging, and model training—segregated from commercial production workloads—are frequently claimed where directly incremental to experimental work, although claimants must ensure general hosting or routine software licences are not double-counted when electing the 55% PPA (and note that under Québec's CRIC rules, cloud server rental fees are ineligible unless hardware is purchased and capitalized).

Across all claim methods, ITR Section 2902 (paragraphs 2902(a)–(d)) bars ITC claims on prescribed expenditures, including: general business administration or management salaries and expenses; legal or accounting fees (subject to Budget 2026's proposed future carve-out for IP registration/maintenance); interest and other financing costs; dues or membership fees in scientific or technical societies; acquisitions of used equipment; acquisitions of rights; donations; reimbursements; and outlays incurred to earn income exempt from Part I tax. Depreciation and Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) are likewise strictly ineligible as SR&ED expenditures.
4.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Lease Costs, and Shared-Use Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024)

Enacted through Bill C-15 and detailed in CRA's updated SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026) and SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), capital property acquired after December 15, 2024 and equipment lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024 once again qualify for SR&ED tax incentives (whereas capital property or usage rights acquired before December 16, 2024 remain strictly excluded). Capital assets claimed under SR&ED must not be included in CCA schedules on Schedule 8, and claimants must report up to the 10 most expensive SR&ED depreciable properties claimed on Line 390—along with each asset's percentage of total operating time—on Lines 262 and 263 of Form T661 (26).

body.text: To illustrate CRA's SUE ITC and recapture rules from the May 22, 2026 Shared-Use-Equipment Policy: if a CCPC acquires new qualifying SUE on February 13, 2025 for $160,000 at the 35% ITC rate and uses it primarily (>50%) for Canadian SR&ED across both the 12-month and 24-month periods, it earns a First-Term ITC of 35% × ($160,000 × 25%) = $14,000 and a Second-Term ITC of 35% × ($160,000 × 25%) = $14,000, totalling $28,000. If the asset is sold in 2028 for $100,000, SUE recapture equals the lesser of $28,000 (total ITC obtained) and 35% × (50% × $100,000) = $17,500, adding $17,500 to income tax payable in 2028.
4.6 Proposed Commercialization and IP Protection Expenditures (Budget 2026)

Under Federal Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026, pp. 117, 127, 402–403, 420–421), for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026 (subject to legislative enactment), the federal government proposes to expand SR&ED eligible costs to cover two downstream commercialization categories within existing 35% and 15% credit rates. First, regulatory and certification work—comprising tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for the initial approval or certification of a product or process—will qualify where directly tied to an eligible SR&ED project, using standard SR&ED cost categories (salaries/wages, materials, contracts, overhead, and machinery/equipment). Second, intellectual property protection costs incurred to register and maintain protection for IP developed during an eligible SR&ED project—specifically patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and registered copyrights in software, including application preparation, filing, and periodic maintenance fees in Canada or abroad—will become eligible SR&ED expenditures, provided the support activities occur in Canada. Litigation and patent enforcement costs remain strictly excluded, general commercialization/marketing unrelated to eligible SR&ED remains barred, disposing of the IP triggers recapture of related SR&ED deductions and ITCs, and the CRA will publish sector-specific administrative guidance to clarify eligibility boundaries.
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Nine provinces and Yukon supplement federal SR&ED with sub-national R&D tax credits, while Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut offer none. Because every provincial or territorial R&D tax credit (unless validly waived or renounced) constitutes government assistance under ITA subsection 127(9), it reduces the federal SR&ED deductible pool and qualified expenditure base dollar-for-dollar, creating an interdependent calculation cascade.
5.1 Québec: Transition to the CRIC Regime, CDAEIA, and DICI Patent Deduction

Administered autonomously by Revenu Québec, Québec's innovation tax landscape underwent a sweeping consolidation in the 2025–2026 Québec Budget tabled on March 25, 2025 (Information Bulletin 2025-6). For taxation years and fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec repealed eight separate R&D tax credits—including the former R&D Salaries and Wages Credit (14% base / 30% enhanced on Form RD-1029.7-V), the University/Public Research Centre Credit (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), the Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research Credit (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V), and the Research Consortium Fees Credit (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V, whose cumulative prior fee balance remains claimable only for taxation years ending no later than December 31, 2029)—replacing them with the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation).

Restricted to corporations (and corporate members of partnerships) operating a business with an establishment in Québec, the CRIC is 100% refundable regardless of corporate size or CCPC status, paying 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding an annual exclusion threshold, and 20% on all qualified expenditures above $1,000,000. The exclusion threshold equals the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec personal income tax basic personal amount for each eligible employee, adjusted pro rata for the time spent on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. Crucially, provided upstream R&D is conducted in Québec, CRIC covers downstream pre-commercialization continuations, namely: (1) regulatory tests, technological validations, and studies aimed at obtaining initial commercialization approval or certification; and (2) product design (development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials). Qualified CRIC expenditures comprise 100% of Québec employee wages, 50% of Québec subcontractor contracts, 50% of payments to eligible Québec universities, public research centres, or research consortia, and 100% of capitalized property acquisition costs (excluding land and buildings; practitioner guidance notes equipment must be capitalized and used in Québec for at least two years, with >90% R&D usage for R&D assets, while uncapitalized cloud server rental fees are excluded). Corporations claim CRIC by attaching Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (and Form RD-222-V for R&D deductions) to their Québec corporate income tax return.

CRIC cannot be combined on the same dollar of expenditure with other Québec tax credits, such as the fully refundable C3i investment and innovation credit (15%, 20%, or 25% by regional economic vitality) or the CDAEIA—which replaced Québec's legacy e-business credit (CDAE) for fiscal years starting after December 31, 2025 to subsidize corporations integrating artificial intelligence features at 30% of eligible IT salaries above an exclusion threshold (split 22% refundable and 8% non-refundable in 2026, shifting to 21%/9% in 2027 and 20%/10% from 2028, subject to an annual Investissement Québec certificate). On downstream IP profits, Québec's DICI deduction taxes qualifying Québec IP commercialization income at an effective 2% corporate rate instead of 11.5%.
5.2 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC Three-Tier Architecture

Administered by the CRA under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), Ontario provides three stackable corporate R&D tax credits for corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment (each requiring a timely filed federal Form T661). First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566) pays an 8% fully refundable credit to qualifying CCPCs on up to $3,000,000 of annual Ontario qualified SR&ED expenditures (maximum credit $240,000/year, shared across associated corporations and prorated for short tax years). While Ontario harmonized with Bill C-15 by restoring 100% of qualified capital expenditures acquired on or after December 16, 2024, Ontario did NOT increase its $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit to $6,000,000, and continues to phase out the $3,000,000 limit under two compounding prior-year associated-group grinds: federal taxable income between $500,000 and $800,000, and specified/taxable capital employed in Canada between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Under subsection 96(14) of the Taxation Act, 2007, a corporation may waive OITC in whole or in part by filing a written waiver with its return within six months of tax year-end (or on an amended return).

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit to all corporations (CCPCs, public companies, and foreign subsidiaries) with no expenditure limit, carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years. Crucially, the OITC is government assistance that reduces the ORDTC base before the 3.5% rate is applied, and both OITC and ORDTC subsequently reduce federal qualified expenditures. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedules 568 & 569) provides a 20% fully refundable credit on qualified contract payments to eligible Ontario universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, or Centres of Excellence, up to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap (maximum credit $4,000,000/year).
5.3 British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Canada, and Yukon
Across Western, Prairie, Atlantic, and Northern Canada, provincial and territorial R&D regimes display distinct structural designs as of November 2026:

items: British Columbia (Income Tax Act (B.C.) Part 6, ss. 97–103 & Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026 — Form T666): Following BC Budget 2026 (February 17, 2026), Bill 2 made BC's 10% SR&ED tax credit permanent (eliminating its statutory expiry date) and aligned with federal Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 by raising the refundable expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 ($15M–$75M prior-year taxable capital phase-out), restoring capital expenditure eligibility, and extending the 10% refundable tier to ECPCs alongside CCPCs (up to $600,000/year refundable). Excess expenditures and claims by non-CCPC/non-ECPC corporations (including active corporate partnership members) earn a 10% non-refundable credit carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years (non-refundable amounts may be renounced). Form T666 must be filed within a strict, non-extendable 18 months of tax year-end.

Alberta (Innovation Employment Grant — AT1 Schedule 29 / Form AT29 & Form AT4970): Administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) and made permanent in Alberta's 2025 budget according to grant-tracking publications, the IEG is a 100% refundable tax credit on up to $4,000,000 of annual Alberta R&D spending matching federal SR&ED rules (maximum payout $800,000/year), paying 8% up to the corporation's base level of spending (its average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding two taxation years) and an enhanced 20% on incremental spending above that two-year average. Eligibility phases out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of taxable capital, and claims are due 15 months after the corporation's filing due date.

Saskatchewan (R&D Tax Credit — Schedule 403 & SCII Patent Box): Saskatchewan's March 18, 2026 budget enhanced its 10% R&D credit (aligning effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) by doubling the 10% refundable CCPC cap from $1,000,000 to the first $2,000,000 of eligible expenditures (one-third of the federal limit) and restoring capital expenditure and equipment lease eligibility. Excess CCPC spending and non-CCPC claims earn a 10% non-refundable credit (carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years per practitioner guides, though one startup summary cites 20 years), subject to a $1,000,000 combined annual credit ceiling across refundable and non-refundable tiers. Separately, Saskatchewan's Commercial Innovation Incentive (SCII) Patent Box (continuous intake; current sunset reported as June 30, 2027) reduces provincial corporate income tax from 12% to 6% for 10 consecutive years—or 15 years if at least 50% of R&D occurred in Saskatchewan—on qualifying new-to-Canada patents, plant breeders' rights, trade secrets, and software algorithm copyrights.

Manitoba (Income Tax Act (Manitoba) s. 7.3 — Schedule 380): Provides an uncapped 15% credit on Manitoba current expenditures, depreciable capital property (excluding buildings and leasehold interests), and First/Second-Term SUE. For in-house R&D, half (7.5%) is refundable and half (7.5%) is non-refundable (carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years, with optional renunciation under s. 7.3(7)); R&D under eligible contracts with qualifying Manitoba institutes is 15% fully refundable.

Atlantic Canada and Yukon: Nova Scotia (s. 41, Schedule 340, 18-month deadline, renunciation within 6 months of year-end), New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador (s. 42, 12 months after filing due date, uniquely open to individuals, trusts, and partners as well as corporations, and not reduced by non-GST/HST government assistance), and Yukon (12 months after filing due date, 15% refundable plus 5% bonus = 20% on payments to Yukon University) all provide uncapped 15% fully refundable R&D tax credits.

body.text: 6. Direct Innovation Grants, Government Assistance, and Stacking Mechanics
6.1 Subsection 127(9) Government Assistance Rules and Bill C-69 Loan Exemption

Under ITA subsection 127(9), any "government assistance" (grants, non-repayable contributions, subsidies, forgivable loans, or provincial tax credits) and "non-government assistance" that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably expect to receive in respect of SR&ED reduces both the Section 37 deductible SR&ED pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures dollar-for-dollar. Subsequent repayments of government assistance increase qualified expenditures in the year repaid. Crucially, however, as confirmed in CRA's January 28, 2025 policy update implementing Bill C-69, subsection 127(9) of the ITA was amended so that bona fide loans from public authorities in Canada with reasonable repayment terms are generally no longer treated as government assistance, effective retroactively for loans made after December 31, 2019. Taxpayers that previously reduced Form T661 qualified expenditures for post-2019 bona fide government loans may amend returns for taxation years that are not statute-barred.
6.2 Major Complementary Programs and Multi-Program Stacking Calculations

Canadian firms regularly layer prospective R&D grants ahead of retrospective SR&ED claims (respecting federal treasury stacking rules that generally cap combined direct government grant contributions at 75% of eligible project costs, or 80% under Québec's ESSOR program). NRC IRAP (Industrial Research Assistance Program), delivered through more than 250 Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) to incorporated, for-profit Canadian SMEs with 500 or fewer FTE employees, provides non-repayable contributions (service standards cover up to $10,000,000, with a median award reported at ~$75,000, typically reimbursing 60%–80% of internal technical salaries and 50% of subcontractors; Budget 2026 proposed $298 million over three years from 2027–28 to renew IRAP Clean Technology). IRAP must be approved before project work commences, and CRA cross-references IRAP disbursements against Form T661 assistance disclosures. Similarly, Mitacs Accelerate co-funds academic research internships at $15,000 per 4–6 month internship ($20,000 for postdocs), requiring a 50% private-sector corporate contribution ($7,500 or $10,000, never paid from government grants), while ISED's Strategic Response Fund (formerly the Strategic Innovation Fund — SIF) received $1 billion over six years starting in 2028–29 in Budget 2026 for large-scale AI, biomanufacturing, agri-food, and cleantech projects.

Because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the Proxy Method is computed on gross eligible directly engaged SR&ED salaries before deducting IRAP salary grants or provincial credits, combining grants and provincial credits with federal SR&ED yields substantial net leverage across four 2026 CCPC scenarios below:

To implement Royal Assent of Bill C-15, the CRA issued updated prescribed SR&ED forms in May 2026 alongside interim line-by-line instructions while Guide T4088 (Guide to Form T661) undergoes comprehensive revision:

body.text: 7.2 Absolute Statutory Filing Deadlines and the Pre-Claim Approval Process

Taxpayers must file Form T661 and Schedule 31 (or T2038-IND) within 12 months after the income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year—giving corporations 18 months (6 months to file T2 plus 12 months; e.g., a December 31, 2025 year-end must file by June 30, 2027) and individuals 17.5 months from the end of the taxation year. This statutory reporting deadline is absolute, with zero CRA administrative extensions; missing the 18-month / 17.5-month cutoff permanently forfeits the claim for that taxation year.

To provide upfront certainty prior to filing, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026. Eligible businesses submit an application via My Business Account before starting R&D work or incurring costs, receiving a formal CRA eligibility determination within eight (8) weeks (practitioner summaries note approvals hold for up to three years unless project work materially changes), supported by one-on-one CRA outreach sessions (OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca) and First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS) guidance.
7.3 CRA Review Procedures, Service Standards, Disputes, and Penalties

Every SR&ED claim is risk-assessed upon receipt of a complete claim and income tax return, and once selected for review, a claim cannot be withdrawn. CRA service standards target 60 calendar days for claims accepted as filed, 90 calendar days for refundable claims selected for review where every project holds Pre-Claim Approval, 180 calendar days for standard refundable claims selected for review, and 365 calendar days for non-refundable reviewed claims. Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated October 29, 2025), reviews pair a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (evaluating technical eligibility under a Research and Technology Manager, RTM) with a Financial Reviewer (FR) (auditing costs under a Financial Review Manager, FRM). Following an initial scoping call and written Request for Information (generally carrying a 30-day deadline), reviewers interview technical performers (virtually or on-site; note CRA manual rules require immediate termination of any meeting if unauthorized recording is discovered) and issue a Proposal Letter granting 30 days to respond before assessment.

Disagreements during review follow CRA's three-step administrative pathway (AP SR&ED 2000-02R): (1) discussion with the RTA or FR; (2) escalation to the RTM or FRM; and (3) an Administrative Second Review. Crucially, an Administrative Second Review does NOT pause the statutory objection clock: to preserve legal appeal rights, the claimant must file a formal Notice of Objection with the Chief of Appeals within 90 calendar days of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment date, before appealing to the Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal. Non-compliance exposes claimants and consultants to the $1,000 claim preparer penalty under ITA subsection 162(5.1) (where contingency fees typically run 15%–30% of credits) and gross negligence penalties under ITA subsection 163(2) / paragraph 163(2)(d) on overstated SR&ED claims.
8. Landmark Canadian Jurisprudence and Evidentiary Standards
8.1 The Binding Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie, and C.W. Agencies

The bedrock judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1) was established by Judge Bowman (later Chief Justice Bowman) in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC)), endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 D.T.C. 5087, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 235 N.R. 258 (FCA), para. 10) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393, [2002] 1 C.T.C. 212, para. 17). Every claimed SR&ED project must affirmatively satisfy five cumulative criteria on a balance of probabilities:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?

Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?
Did the process result in a technological advancement (advancing technological understanding or capability)?
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: 8.2 Appellate Reaffirmation, Routine Engineering, and Contemporaneous Evidence Precedents

Subsequent appellate and trial jurisprudence has consistently reinforced both the strictness and the evidentiary pragmatism of the Northwest Hydraulic framework. Following earlier FCA confirmations in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 FCA 355, aff'g 2011 TCC 261) and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. (2016 FCA), as well as Tax Court applications such as Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6, Justice Sommerfeldt, scrutinizing the Fire Curtain and Manual Override projects) and Clevor Technologies Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen (2019 TCC 166, Justice Russell), taxpayers challenged Criterion #3 at the appellate level by arguing that the phrase "scientific method" does not appear in subsection 248(1) and that CRA's August 2021 administrative guidelines ("Why" and "How" questions) softened the test. In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88), the Federal Court of Appeal rejected the first argument, and in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72, aff'g 2020 TCC 47) it unanimously rejected both, holding that statutory interpretation belongs exclusively to the courts, that CRA guidelines did not remove the requirement to follow the scientific method, and that even where technological uncertainty exists (as found in National R&D), a claim fails if systematic hypothesis testing and progressive records are absent. National R&D also established a critical litigation warning: expert witness reports are inadmissible where an expert abandons impartiality, attempts to introduce unproven facts through the back door, or opines directly on the ultimate legal question of SR&ED eligibility.

Conversely, recent Tax Court of Canada decisions protect genuine SME innovators against overly rigid documentary formalism. Building on Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313, para. 94)—which held that "the existence of contemporaneous documentation, or contemporaneous documents with specific content, is not a condition to the recognition of scientific research or experimental development"—the Tax Court in DAZZM Inc. v. The King (2024 TCC 129, para. 119) explicitly confirmed that although the CRA "would have liked to see contemporaneous time sheets for the work performed, they are not necessarily required for work to be eligible as qualifying SRED" where credible alternative evidence substantiates the work. Most recently, in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025 TCC), the Tax Court allowed a food-science formulation appeal ("Chrisoda") in full after the taxpayer proved on a balance of probabilities across all five Northwest Hydraulic questions that standard procedures could not resolve its technological uncertainty and that it followed a systematic scientific method. In practice, pairing contemporaneous architecture decision records, Git commit logs, failed-experiment logs, segmented R&D cloud billing, and project-linked timesheets—and separately tracking regulatory certification tests and IP filing invoices ahead of the November 5, 2026 commercialization expansion—remains the gold standard for Canadian SR&ED audit defence.
